analysis.one_liner: Imposes a 70% tax on pay above $1 million at companies that took big federal bailouts.
analysis.headline: The bill never got a hearing or a vote; it died in the House Ways and Means Committee with 5 total supporters.
analysis.plain_summary: The bill would add a 70% surtax on any compensation above $1 million paid to employees or former employees of companies that received more than $500 million in federal bailout money through the 2008 financial rescue programs. The tax would apply retroactively to pay received after the end of 2007, and would end once a company fully repaid the government. Executives who returned the money, held employer stock under certain rules, or earned straight sales commissions would be exempt. It was referred to the tax-writing committee and never moved again.
analysis.who_benefits: Taxpayers who funded the 2008 bailouts. The tax would claw back a share of large pay packages at banks and other firms rescued with more than $500 million of public money, and pressure those firms to limit payouts while they still owed the government.
analysis.who_benefits_short: Taxpayers who funded the bank bailouts

how_it_helps.text: The bill imposes a 70% tax on compensation above $1 million received from any company that took more than $500 million in TARP or housing-rescue funds, applying to pay received after December 31, 2007 [S2][S3].
The tax covers all forms of pay, including unsecured loans, and counts money parked in creditor-protected trusts as paid to the employee, so pay could not simply be re-labeled to escape it [S3].
The tax ends once a company fully repays the government, so it targets firms while they still owe taxpayers, not companies that have cleaned up their balance sheets [S3].
Employees who return the money within 60 days would not owe the tax, giving executives a path to simply give the pay back [S3].

analysis.who_pays: Top executives and highly paid employees of the largest bailout recipients — big banks and mortgage-finance firms — who would owe the 70% surtax on pay above $1 million while their employers remained on government life support. Their companies would face pressure to cut or restructure large pay packages.

drawbacks.text: The tax applies retroactively to pay received after 2007, which is exactly the kind of after-the-rules-change taxation that critics of retroactive taxes warn against, even when aimed at unpopular recipients [S3].

A 70% surtax limited to bailout recipients could push top talent out of the rescued firms or into aggressive pay restructuring at the moment the government was trying to stabilize them, a cost honest supporters would have to weigh [S3].
The bill carves out commissions for salespeople and allows some stock compensation under regulation, exceptions that reduce how much large pay it actually reaches [S2][S3].

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: The policy goal — recouping some of the pay at firms rescued with public money — was popular after the 2008 crash, and the bill included escape hatches (returning the money, repaying the bailout ends the tax) that softened the harshest objections. The retroactive application and the risk of destabilizing pay at fragile firms are real costs, but the main problem was that Congress never debated them: the bill got no hearing, no markup, and no vote.

outcome.mechanism: It was sent to the House Ways and Means Committee the day it was introduced and never came out; the Congress ended with no hearing, no vote, and no action of any kind.

narrative.text: Rep. Brad Sherman introduced the bill on March 30, 2009, with four Democratic cosponsors: Reps. Kaptur, Filner, Kucinich, and DeFazio [S1][S4].
The same day, the bill was referred to the House Committee on Ways and Means, the committee that handles tax legislation [S5].

That referral was the last action ever taken on the bill; no subcommittee or full committee action, floor vote, or Senate consideration followed before the 111th Congress ended on January 3, 2011 [S5].

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Executives at the largest bailout recipients kept their full pay packages, untouched by any tax, because the bill never left committee. The tax-writing committee's agenda, not the bill's 5 supporters or its opponents, decided that.

for.name: Brad Sherman
for.what_they_did: Introduced the bill imposing a 70% tax on pay above $1 million at companies that received more than $500 million in bailout funds.

for.name: 4 of 253 House Democrats
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill (Reps. Kaptur, Filner, Kucinich, and DeFazio).

against.name: House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: Received the bill by referral on the day it was introduced and took no further action — no hearing, no markup, no vote — for the rest of the Congress.

against.name: Charles Rangel
against.role: Chair, House Ways and Means Committee
against.what_they_did: As committee chair, never scheduled the bill for consideration; the bill sat without action until the Congress ended.

sides.party_line_note: All five supporters were Democrats, and the bill never drew a Republican cosponsor or a floor vote, so any broader partisan split was never tested.

industries.industry: Large banks and mortgage-finance firms that received over $500 million in TARP or housing-rescue funds
industries.note: The bill would have imposed a 70% surtax on their executives' pay above $1 million until they fully repaid the government. It died in committee, so nothing changed for them.

Because the bill never advanced, executives at rescued firms kept pay packages above $1 million without the proposed surtax. Their interest in the bill's failure ran directly against the taxpayers who funded the bailouts.
